answerSpec.modelAnswer: After Germany let its treaty with Russia lapse in 1890, Russia allied with France in 1894, so Germany faced possible enemies on both its western and eastern borders and the danger of a war on two fronts. Britain, which Germans had hoped would stay apart, then settled its colonial quarrels with France in 1904 and with Russia in 1907, and at the Algeciras Conference in 1906 it backed France against Germany. By 1907 France, Russia and Britain were linked in the Triple Entente. Germany's only reliable ally was Austria-Hungary, since Italy was on good terms with France and Britain. Many Germans blamed encirclement on their enemies, but German policies such as Weltpolitik and the naval building programme had themselves pushed Britain towards France and Russia.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The alliance system was an important cause. By 1907 Europe was divided into the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente, and Germany felt encircled by France and Russia. In July 1914 the alliances helped turn a quarrel between Austria-Hungary and Serbia into a general war: Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria-Hungary, and France stood by Russia.

However, other causes were at least as important. The arms race created fear, and the Schlieffen Plan meant that war with Russia automatically became war with France through Belgium. Colonial crises in Morocco had poisoned relations, and Balkan nationalism threatened Austria-Hungary. The alliances also did not force anyone to fight: Italy stayed neutral although it was in the Triple Alliance, and Britain had no binding promise to France. The decisions of July 1914 mattered most: Germany's blank cheque, Austria-Hungary's ultimatum and Russia's general mobilisation were choices made by leaders.

I disagree that the alliances were the main cause. They explain how the war spread, but the war began because of the Balkan crisis and the decisions taken in July 1914, made more dangerous by military plans.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Colonial problems did create tension. The two Moroccan crises of 1905-06 and 1911 brought France and Germany close to war, and each time Britain stood by France, so the entente grew closer and Germany felt isolated. Germany resented being denied a 'place in the sun', and the Fashoda crisis of 1898 had shown that colonial disputes could set even Britain and France against each other.

However, colonial tension had limits. Every colonial crisis was settled by negotiation, and by 1913-14 Britain and Germany had reached agreements over the Baghdad railway and Portugal's colonies. Other problems caused deeper tension: the Bosnian crisis humiliated Russia, the Balkan Wars doubled Serbia's size and alarmed Austria-Hungary, and the naval race turned Britain against Germany.

Overall, colonial problems created serious tension, especially by shaping the Anglo-French entente, but they were less dangerous than the Balkans, which involved the survival and prestige of Great Powers and produced the crisis of 1914.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Belgian resistance played a part. The forts of Liège held out for about twelve days, and the Belgians blew up railways and bridges, delaying a plan that had no time to spare. Even more important, the invasion of Belgium brought Britain into the war, and the BEF delayed the Germans again at Mons.

Joffre's counter-attack at the Marne then forced the Germans to retreat.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Both battles showed the terrible cost of attrition. Historians estimate roughly 700,000 casualties at Verdun, and on the first day of the Somme alone the British suffered about 57,000 casualties, with over a million on all sides by November. answerSpec.modelAnswer:
New methods of warfare did help to break the stalemate in 1918. Tanks, used in large numbers at Cambrai in 1917 and Amiens in 1918, could cross wire and trenches, and aircraft spotted for the artillery and attacked troops on the ground. Above all, the British and French learned to combine infantry, tanks, aircraft and accurate artillery with creeping barrages, which made the Hundred Days so successful.

However, new weapons were not enough on their own. Gas never broke the stalemate because masks soon reduced its effect, and the first tanks of 1916 were slow and unreliable. The stalemate was broken in 1918 also because Germany had lost hundreds of thousands of its best troops in the failed Spring Offensive, American troops were arriving in large numbers, the blockade had weakened Germany, and Foch's unified command let the Allies use their reserves well.

New methods were important, but only when combined with each other and with German exhaustion and American manpower. Their importance lay less in any single weapon than in the new tactics that used them together.

The war on the Western Front began on 4 August 1914, when German armies invaded Belgium under the Schlieffen Plan, which aimed to defeat France in about six weeks by sweeping round Paris. The Belgian forts at Liège held the Germans up for about twelve days. Britain declared war and sent the BEF, which met the German First Army at Mons on 23 August. Its accurate rifle fire delayed the Germans for a day before it joined the long Allied retreat towards Paris.

Meanwhile Russia mobilised faster than expected and invaded East Prussia, so in late August Moltke moved troops east, weakening the right wing in France. Exhausted and short of supplies, the German right wing turned to pass east of Paris instead of round it, exposing its flank. Joffre counter-attacked at the Marne from 6 to 12 September, helped by the BEF and reserves rushed from Paris. The Germans retreated to the River Aisne and dug trenches on high ground, and the Schlieffen Plan had failed.

Each side now tried to outflank the other to the north in the race to the sea, until the lines reached the Channel coast. At the First Battle of Ypres, from October to November, the Germans tried to break through to the Channel ports; the British, French and Belgians held on, but most of Britain's regular army was killed or wounded. By December 1914 continuous lines of trenches ran from the North Sea to Switzerland. The war of movement was over, and a war of attrition had begun.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The Battle of the Somme, fought from 1 July to November 1916, was important in several different ways.

In military terms, it achieved some of its aims. It began partly to relieve pressure on the French at Verdun, and German attacks there were reduced once the Somme began. It also wore down the German army very badly; German commanders were shaken by the losses, and early in 1917 Germany withdrew to the shorter, stronger Hindenburg Line. Some historians therefore see it as an important step in the attrition that eventually exhausted Germany.

However, judged by ground gained, it was a failure. The Allies advanced at most about ten kilometres and there was no breakthrough. Its human cost was enormous: on the first day alone the British army suffered about 57,000 casualties, nearly 20,000 of them killed, and total casualties on all sides are estimated at over a million.

The Somme was also important for the development of warfare. Tanks were used for the first time on 15 September 1916, and the British army learned hard lessons about artillery, the creeping barrage and infantry tactics. Some historians argue that these lessons formed a 'learning curve' that led to the victories of 1918; others argue that the cost of learning was far too high.

For Britain, the Somme was the first great battle of the volunteer armies raised in 1914-15. Because many 'Pals' battalions came from the same towns, whole communities lost their young men in a single day. Its importance in memory has been huge: it shaped the view of the war as futile and of generals such as Haig as careless of their men's lives, a view still debated today.

Compared with other events, its military importance can be questioned. Verdun was more important for France, and the Hundred Days of 1918 actually won the war. But the Somme was important as a turning point in the nature of the war and in how it was remembered.

Overall, the Somme was very important. In the short term it failed to break through and cost terrible losses, but it relieved Verdun, weakened the German army and taught lessons that were used in 1918. In the long term its greatest importance may be in how it shaped British memory of the war.

When war began, Britain, France, Belgium and South Africa attacked Germany's four African colonies. Togoland was captured by British and French forces in August 1914, and Kamerun was conquered after a longer campaign by early 1916.

In southern Africa, South Africa first had to defeat a rebellion by Afrikaners who refused to fight for Britain. South African forces under Louis Botha then invaded German South West Africa, which surrendered in July 1915.

The longest campaign was in German East Africa. The German commander, Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, had a small force made up mostly of African askari, and his aim was to tie down as many British Empire troops as possible. In November 1914 an Indian expeditionary force was badly defeated when it tried to land at Tanga. From 1916 Jan Smuts led a large army of South African, Indian, British and African troops, including the King's African Rifles and later the Rhodesia Native Regiment, which drove the Germans out of most of the colony. Lettow-Vorbeck avoided decisive battles and moved into Portuguese East Africa and then Northern Rhodesia. He surrendered at Abercorn only on 25 November 1918, two weeks after the armistice in Europe.

The campaign depended on African carriers because there were few roads and the tsetse fly killed animals. Estimates vary, but historians commonly suggest that around a million Africans were used as carriers and that more than 100,000 died, mostly of disease, hunger and exhaustion, while villages lost their young men and food, and famine followed in some areas.

The Gallipoli campaign of 1915 was significant in several ways, though less for its effect on the outcome of the war than for its wider consequences.

Its aims were ambitious: to capture Constantinople, knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war and open a sea route to Russia. Its failure meant none of these were achieved. After the naval attack in March and the landings in April and August, the Allies withdrew in January 1916, having suffered heavy losses; historians estimate that each side suffered roughly a quarter of a million casualties. The campaign tied down Ottoman forces, but it achieved no lasting gains.

Strategically, the failure mattered because Russia remained cut off from Allied supplies through the Black Sea. Russia's shortages of weapons and equipment contributed to its defeats and, in the end, to the revolutions of 1917, although many other factors were involved.

Politically, Gallipoli damaged the reputation of Winston Churchill, who had championed the plan and left the Admiralty in 1915. For Australia and New Zealand, it became central to national identity: the sacrifice of the ANZACs is remembered every year on Anzac Day, 25 April. For Turkey, the successful defence made the reputation of Mustafa Kemal, who later founded the Turkish Republic.

There were also military lessons about amphibious landings, which planners studied before the landings of the Second World War.

However, judged by its effect on the outcome of the First World War, Gallipoli was a sideshow. The war was decided on the Western Front, and its failure did not change the balance there.

Overall, Gallipoli was of limited significance for the outcome of the war, but highly significant for its long-term consequences: for Russia's isolation, for the national identities of Australia, New Zealand and Turkey, and for the careers of leaders on both sides.

By September 1918 Germany was losing the war. Since Amiens on 8 August the Allies had driven the German army back, and in late September they broke through the Hindenburg Line. At the end of September Bulgaria asked for an armistice, and on 29 September Ludendorff told the Kaiser that the war was lost and that a new government should ask for peace.

In early October the new Chancellor, Prince Max of Baden, whose government included Social Democrats, asked President Wilson for an armistice based on his Fourteen Points. Wilson's replies made clear that he would not deal with the Kaiser's old regime. Ludendorff, who had changed his mind and wanted to fight on, was dismissed in late October, while the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary signed armistices.

At the end of October the naval command ordered the High Seas Fleet to sea for a final battle. The sailors refused, and in early November the mutiny at Kiel spread. Workers' and soldiers' councils took control in many cities, and a republic was declared in Bavaria. On 9 November Prince Max announced the Kaiser's abdication, the Social Democrat Friedrich Ebert became head of government, and a republic was proclaimed in Berlin. Wilhelm II fled to the Netherlands.

The German delegation, led by Matthias Erzberger, signed the Armistice in a railway carriage at Compiègne early on 11 November, and the fighting stopped at 11 a.m.

The British naval blockade was an important cause of Germany's defeat, though it worked slowly and in combination with other factors.

Its economic effects were serious. From 1914 the Royal Navy stopped imports of food, fertiliser and raw materials. Over time this caused shortages that affected both the war economy and daily life. The winter of 1916-17 became known as the turnip winter, many Germans relied on substitute foods, and estimates suggest hundreds of thousands of extra civilian deaths linked to hunger.

Its social and political effects were perhaps even more important. Hunger fed discontent, strikes and protests against the war, and in 1918 war-weariness helped the Kiel mutiny turn into a revolution. The blockade also affected the army: during the Spring Offensive hungry soldiers stopped to loot Allied supply dumps and discovered that the enemy was well fed, which damaged morale.

The blockade also had an important indirect effect. Germany's answer to it was the U-boat, and its decision in 1917 to return to unrestricted submarine warfare brought the USA into the war.

However, the blockade did not defeat Germany on its own. It worked slowly: Germany fought on for more than four years. The German army was defeated on the battlefield in 1918, when the Spring Offensive failed and cost its best troops, and the Allies, with American help, drove it back in the Hundred Days. The collapse of Bulgaria, the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary also left Germany alone.

Overall, the blockade was very important as a long-term cause of defeat: it weakened the economy, the home front and the army's morale, and indirectly brought in the USA. But the immediate cause of Germany's request for an armistice was military defeat in 1918, which the blockade made more likely but did not by itself bring about.

After France fell in June 1940, Britain refused to make peace, and in July Hitler ordered preparations for an invasion, Operation Sea Lion. An invasion across the Channel needed control of the air, so the Luftwaffe had to defeat RAF Fighter Command first.

In July the Luftwaffe attacked shipping in the Channel and coastal ports. In August it turned to the RAF itself, bombing airfields and radar stations in southern England. These attacks put Fighter Command under heavy strain, with pilots exhausted and airfields damaged. But radar and the RAF's control system allowed fighters to meet raids without wasteful patrols, Spitfires and Hurricanes were a match for German fighters, and pilots from Poland, Czechoslovakia, the dominions and other countries strengthened the RAF. German fighters could stay over England only briefly before their fuel ran low.

On 7 September the Luftwaffe switched to bombing London, starting the Blitz. This relieved the pressure on the RAF's airfields and gave it time to recover. On 15 September large German raids suffered heavy losses, showing that the RAF was far from defeated. Soon afterwards Hitler postponed Sea Lion. Fighting in the air continued into October, but Germany had failed to win air superiority, and the invasion never took place.

The Battle of Stalingrad, from August 1942 to February 1943, was one of the most significant battles of the Second World War.

In military terms its significance was enormous. In November 1942 the Red Army surrounded the German Sixth Army, and after Hitler refused to allow a break-out and the airlift and relief attack failed, Paulus surrendered at the end of January 1943. About 91,000 German soldiers were taken prisoner. For the first time a whole German army had been destroyed. The defeat also ended Germany's 1942 drive towards the oil of the Caucasus, which it badly needed.

Strategically, Stalingrad passed the initiative on the Eastern Front to the Red Army. After the failure of the German offensive at Kursk in July 1943, Germany was on the defensive in the east for the rest of the war, and the Red Army began the advance that took it to Berlin.

Its effect on morale was also significant. German propaganda could not hide the disaster, and many Germans began to see that the war could be lost. For the Soviet people and the Allies, Stalingrad was proof that Germany could be beaten, and it raised the prestige of the USSR and of Stalin.

However, its significance can be compared with other battles. Some historians argue that the defeat before Moscow in December 1941 was the true turning point, because it ended Germany's hopes of a quick victory. Others point to Kursk, the last major German offensive in the east, or to El Alamein in North Africa in the same period.

Overall, Stalingrad was highly significant. Moscow showed that Germany could not win quickly, but Stalingrad showed that it could lose: it destroyed a German army, ended its offensive towards the oilfields, changed morale on both sides and began the shift of initiative to the Red Army that Kursk confirmed.

The Battle of Midway, fought from 4 to 7 June 1942, was one of the most important battles of the Pacific war.

Its immediate military importance was huge. Admiral Yamamoto had hoped to destroy the remaining American carriers, but American codebreakers had identified Midway as his target, and Nimitz's carriers lay in ambush. American dive-bombers caught the Japanese carriers while they were rearming and refuelling. Japan lost four fleet carriers, while the USA lost one, the Yorktown. Japan also lost many experienced pilots and skilled mechanics who could not quickly be replaced.

Strategically, Midway ended Japanese expansion in the central Pacific. From then on Japan was mainly on the defensive, and the initiative passed to the USA, which began its first major offensive at Guadalcanal in August 1942. The battle also showed the value of intelligence: codebreaking turned a battle in which the Americans were outnumbered into a decisive victory.

Its importance grew over time because of American industrial power. The USA could build new carriers and train pilots far faster than Japan, so the gap that Midway opened could never be closed. It also restored American confidence only six months after Pearl Harbor.

However, Midway was not the only turning point. A month earlier the Battle of the Coral Sea had stopped the Japanese advance towards Port Moresby. After Midway, the six-month struggle for Guadalcanal was the first Japanese defeat on land and wore down Japanese ships and aircraft. Some historians argue that once Pearl Harbor had failed to destroy the American carriers, Japan was always likely to lose a long war against the USA.

Overall, Midway was extremely important: it was the battle that ended Japan's ability to attack in the central Pacific and handed the initiative to the USA. Its importance rested on the USA's ability to exploit it, and it was one stage, the most decisive, in a wider turn of the war in 1942.

The Allied invasion of Normandy, Operation Overlord, was planned for two years under the supreme commander, General Eisenhower. Huge numbers of ships, landing craft and supplies were gathered in Britain, together with artificial Mulberry harbours. Operation Fortitude used fake armies and false radio traffic to convince Hitler that the main invasion would come at the Pas-de-Calais.

On the night of 5-6 June 1944 airborne troops landed behind the beaches to seize bridges and protect the flanks. At dawn on 6 June about 156,000 troops landed on five beaches: Utah and Omaha (American), Gold and Sword (British) and Juno (Canadian). At Omaha the Americans suffered heavy losses, but by the end of the day all the beachheads were established. Allied air forces controlled the skies and bombed bridges and railways, and the French Resistance sabotaged communications, so German reinforcements arrived slowly. Disputes among German commanders and Hitler's control of the reserves added to the delay.

In June and July fighting was slow and costly in the hedgerow country of Normandy and around Caen. In late July the Americans broke out, and in August German forces were trapped and destroyed in the Falaise pocket. On 15 August another Allied force landed in southern France. On 25 August Paris was liberated, and the Allies began a rapid advance towards Germany.

The Nuremberg trial of the major Nazi leaders, held from November 1945 to October 1946 by an international tribunal of the USA, Britain, France and the USSR, was significant in several ways.

Its first significance was as an act of justice. Leading Nazis were tried as individuals for conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Twelve were sentenced to death, others were imprisoned and three were acquitted, which showed that the court weighed the evidence rather than simply condemning everyone.

Second, the trial created a huge public record. Documents, films and witnesses made the scale of Nazi crimes, including the Holocaust, known around the world, which made it much harder for anyone to deny what had happened.

Third, it was significant for international law. It established that leaders could be held personally responsible for starting aggressive wars and for crimes against humanity, and that following orders was no defence. It influenced the UN Genocide Convention of 1948 and, much later, the creation of international criminal courts. In the short term it also formed part of the Allied policy of denazification in occupied Germany, and the Tokyo trial of 1946-48 followed the same model.

However, the trials have been criticised. Many Germans, and some others, saw them as 'victors' justice', because Allied actions such as the bombing of cities were not judged, and Soviet judges sat in court although the USSR had committed crimes such as the Katyn massacre. Some of the charges applied new laws to past actions, and the great majority of Nazis were never tried at all.

Overall, the Nuremberg trials were highly significant, less for punishing a small number of leaders than for recording Nazi crimes and creating principles of international law that still matter today, even though their fairness is debated.
